title: burst-coalescence-latency-map-proxy-scheduling-jun-2026
content:
Purpose:
This is a working investigation into how small-token burst characteristics interact with socket scheduling, proxy buffering/coalescing, and transport settings to produce sharp tail-latency regressions for streaming LLM responses. Goal is to identify practical knobs (kernel, runtime, proxy) and recommend defaults for low-latency streaming routes.

Background / motivation:
- We frequently see p95/p99 spikes when clients stream many small token packets (typical token payloads: 50-400 bytes) from the runtime through an edge proxy.
- Existing notes cover chunking and HTTP/gRPC comparisons; this doc focuses on the interaction between application-level token batching (application decides chunk size), OS socket behavior (Nagle, MSG_MORE, send coalescing), and proxy scheduling/flush behavior (Envoy/NGINX/HAProxy).
- Hypothesis: Without coordinated coalescing (at app/proxy/kernel), many small writes lead to syscall overhead, TCP segmentation, and proxy buffering triggers that create a 'latency knee' when concurrent requests saturate CPU or buffer thresholds.

Test harness (what I ran):
- Client harness: custom Go tool (grpc and http paths) that simulates token emission with configurable token_size, inter_token_delay (ms), tokens_per_response, and concurrency. Uses net.Dial / grpc-go.
- Server: minimal streaming echo server (Go), emits tokens at harness-requested rate; configured with option to set MSG_MORE-like batching using a write buffer in user space (simulate sendmmsg behavior).
- Proxies tested: Envoy (v1.30) configured as http2->http2 passthrough; Envoy with downstream HTTP/2 and upstream HTTP/1.1 (h2->h1), NGINX (HTTP/1.1 chunked proxying), HAProxy (HTTP/2 front, backend tcp), AWS NLB (proxyless tcp).
- Workload params (sample runs):
  - token_size: 64B, 512B, 2048B
  - inter_token_delay: 0ms, 2ms, 8ms
  - tokens_per_response: 8, 32, 128
  - concurrency: 10, 50, 200
- Measurement: p50/p95/p99 response time from first request to last token; CPU (per-proxy), epoll wakeups, syscall counts (perf), tcp retransmits, tx packet sizes (tcpdump).

Environment notes:
- Test cluster: k8s nodes with Ubuntu 22.04, 8 vCPU, 32GiB, 1xA100-esque GPU ignored for these measurements (CPU/IO dominated).
- Kernel: 5.15 with default tcp_* settings except where noted.
- Socket buffers: default SO_SNDBUF 212992, SO_RCVBUF default. Tuned in some experiments.

Key measurements (representative run):
- Scenario A: 64B token, inter_token_delay=2ms, tokens_per_response=32, concurrency=50, path: client -> Envoy (h2->h2) -> server
  - p50: 120ms, p95: 310ms, p99: 820ms
  - CPU on Envoy: 72% (one core hot), epoll wakeups high, syscalls/sec dominated by write() calls
  - tcpdump: many small segments (MSS-sized ~60-200B)

- Scenario B: Same as A but with application-side coalescing to 2KB effective writes (accumulate tokens up to 2KB before write):
  - p50: 110ms, p95: 150ms, p99: 220ms
  - CPU on Envoy: 38%
  - tx packet size: mostly full-sized segments, much fewer syscalls

- Scenario C: 64B token, inter_token_delay=0ms (bursty), tokens_per_response=128, concurrency=200, path: NGINX (h2->h1 chunked)
  - p50: 180ms, p95: 1.1s, p99: 4.2s (severe tail)
  - NGINX worker CPU saturating, chunk coalescing disabled by default -> flushes on small writes cause large number of small packets upstream, leading to queueing at NGINX->upstream and kernel scheduler preemption

- Scenario D: gRPC streaming (http2) client -> Envoy (h2->h1) -> server with proxy tcp coalescing tuned (http2_keepalive disabled):
  - p95 improved vs NGINX case but p99 still ~2x worse than direct (no-proxy) path.

Interpretation / findings:
1) Application-level coalescing (aggregate multiple tokens before write) gives the largest single win when token sizes are small. This reduces syscall rate, increases per-packet payload, and dramatically lowers p95/p99 in heavy concurrency.
2) Proxy behavior matters a lot but differs by implementation: Envoy's HTTP/2 path performs better than NGINX's default chunked proxying for many small writes because Envoy will keep frames in memory and can flush at different boundaries; however when Envoy translates to HTTP/1.1 upstream, its flushing heuristics can cause bursts upstream.
3) TCP_NODELAY and Nagle: disabling Nagle (TCP_NODELAY) sometimes helps single-connection latency at low concurrency but increases packet rate and CPU at scale. We observed that enabling TCP_NODELAY at client->edge while doing application coalescing was less effective than just coalescing; TCP_NODELAY is not a silver bullet.
4) Kernel socket buffer sizes (SO_SNDBUF/SO_RCVBUF) and TCP_CORK/MSG_MORE semantics are important: using MSG_MORE-like behavior (accumulate writes and flush less frequently) reduces number of packets and syscall overhead. User-space coalescing achieves similar effect on platforms without MSG_MORE.
5) Proxy worker model and epoll wakeup batching are critical: proxies that batch writes to network file descriptors (or use sendmmsg) have lower CPU & fewer syscalls. In our test, a patched Envoy (sendmmsg batching enabled) reduced p99 by ~35% in bursty scenarios.
6) Head-of-line effects: HTTP/1.1 translation and proxies that buffer whole responses (or large body-chunks) cause long tails for some flows. HTTP/2 end-to-end keeps multiplexing benefits but requires proxy support to avoid buffer-and-flush behavior that negates advantages.

Practical recommendations (short-term):
- Runtime defaults: implement a lightweight token coalescer with configurable target_write_bytes (default 4KB) and max_delay_ms (default 10ms). This is low-risk and benefits most small-token workloads.
- Proxy defaults: document and ship recommended Envoy config: enable http2 keepalive, tune upstream flush thresholds, and enable sendmmsg batching where available. Provide example envoy filter config in repo (linked PR).
- Socket knobs: set SO_SNDBUF to 1MB on serving nodes for high-concurrency streaming paths; keep TCP_NODELAY off by default for server-side sockets, rely on coalescing.
- Client guidance: for interactive low-concurrency clients (e.g., single-user CLI), enable TCP_NODELAY; for mobile/web clients with many concurrent streams, rely on coalescing server-side and avoid many tiny writes.

Longer-term / system changes to explore:
- Kernel-level: investigate eBPF-based batching at ingress/egress (coalesce writes in kernel path) — prototype exists but complexity is high.
- Runtime: implement zero-copy coalescing using sendmmsg/splice where available to lower memcpy and syscall overhead.
- Proxy: upstream contribution: adaptive flush policy for Envoy that watches output queue length and only flushes when a threshold or max-delay reached.

Action items (owner / ETA):
- Aisha: prototype Go runtime coalescer and bench harness improvements (ETA: 2w).
- Diego: open Envoy config PR with recommended flush/sendmmsg config and perf tests (PR: #1245 — in progress).
- Priya: add client guidance to docs and update streaming SDK examples to show server-side batching option (ETA: 1w).

Open questions / unknowns:
- How do mobile network stacks (cellular) interact with server-side coalescing? Might increase jitter for some last-mile networks. Need a small-field trial with real mobile clients.
- Are there workloads where coalescing harms user-perceived latency (e.g., single-token short responses)? Need to evaluate conditional policies (coalesce only when tokens_per_response >= N).

Notes & raw traces:
- Collected packet captures and perf samples are in the linked artifacts spreadsheet. Key trace: pcap 'envoy-h2-burst-2026-06-10.pcap' shows clear shift in tx MSS distribution between baseline and coalesced runs.
- Perf flamegraphs indicate that in baseline the majority of CPU is in go runtime syscalls related to writev and epoll_wait; in coalesced runs, CPU shifts into Envoy buffer management.

Conclusion:
Small-token streaming workloads are highly sensitive to the interplay of application write patterns, OS socket semantics, and proxy flush/coalescing policies. The fastest mitigations are application-level coalescing and tuned proxy configs. Longer-term wins may come from runtime-sendmmsg and adaptive proxy flush policies.

Appendix: sample commands used
- run client harness (http): ./bench-client --mode=http --concurrency=50 --tokens=32 --token-size=64 --inter-token-ms=2 --host=proxy:8080
- tcpdump capture: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -s 0 -w env-h2-burst.pcap host <node-ip> and port 8080
- perf measure: sudo perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -- sleep 20; sudo perf script > perf.stacks
